Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for
an Open World

Ruiyao Xu    Yanfei Chen Affiliation: Google Cloud AI Research    Zhongying CuiZhu Affiliation: Google Cloud AI Research    Bhavana Dalvi Mishra Affiliation: Google Cloud AI Research    Yifei Ming Affiliation: Google Cloud AI Research    Han Yu Affiliation: Google Cloud AI Research    Rujun Han Affiliation: Google Cloud AI Research    Chen-Yu Lee Affiliation: Google Cloud AI Research    Tomas Pfister Corresponding author: ruiyaoxu2028@u.northwestern.edu, {yanfeichen, cuizz, chenyulee}@google.com Affiliation: Google Cloud AI Research Affiliation: Northwestern University
Abstract

LLM agents’ capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task’s harness using a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model–harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

1 Introduction

An LLM agent’s effectiveness depends not only on its underlying model, but also on its harness: the prompts, memory, skills, tools, and orchestration through which the model performs tasks (OpenAI, 2025; SST, 2024; Weng, 2026). Even a strong model can perform substantially differently under different harnesses (Team et al., 2026). As agents expand beyond coding into office workflows and high-stakes domains such as legal work, harness design must accommodate increasingly diverse tasks and operational requirements (Team et al., 2026; Harvey AI, 2026). Manually designing and refining harnesses for these demands requires repeated engineering effort, motivating recursive self-improvement on harness design (Lee et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2026; Weng, 2026; Meng et al., 2026). Recursive self-improvement (RSI) pursues AI that improves AI: a system autonomously makes persistent changes to itself, and these changes further shape how later improvements are generated, evaluated, and retained (Duan et al., 2026).

Early harness RSI methods (Lee et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026) focus on optimizing candidate components against fixed training tasks, unit tests, or validation feedback, selecting the best configuration before deployment. However, a static harness selected beforehand often fails to generalize to the diverse, unpredictable environments encountered in the open world (Wang et al., 2026a), a dynamic setting where agents continually encounter new tasks with diverse and evolving requirements. To address this, researchers have moved harness RSI to the open world, allowing systems to dynamically adapt to newly arriving tasks. Current open-world methods typically address this by recursively improving a harness for the current task (Lee et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026a), or by carrying a successful execution harness forward across successive task batches (Nie et al., 2026b).

However, open-world harness evolution faces two connected challenges. First, tasks typically lack ground-truth labels or reliable verifiers. While existing methods rely on proxy signals, assumed ground truth answers, or pairwise output judgments (Lee et al., 2026a; Nie et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026), safely using imperfect execution evidence to guide harness changes remains difficult. Second, improving a harness for one task does not automatically improve how the next task is refined. Task-specific edits often fail when requirements change, and directly inheriting a highly tailored execution harness can cause noisy recursive improvement as task distributions shift. The refinement process itself, however, produces highly reusable experience: how a weakness is diagnosed, which changes are tested, and what their execution reveals. Therefore, the improvement process itself must become a source of learning, enabling the system to recursively upgrade its own refinement mechanism. This leads to our central question:

To this end, we introduce Harness2, a plug-and-play framework for recursive agent harnessing in an open world. We use harnessing to describe the process of optimizing the runtime scaffolding around a frozen base model to enable it to act as an autonomous agent. Harness2 improves the harness for the current task and extracts lessons from that process to guide future harnessing. It implements these updates through two coupled levels of recursion: ❶ Task-level recursion refines the current task’s execution harness. To overcome the absence of ground-truth feedback, we introduce a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step: it proposes harness edits, tests their effects under matched conditions, and composes changes supported by behavioral contrasts. Building on this, parallel recursion explores multiple candidates simultaneously and composes changes from their execution evidence, while sequential recursion builds successive revisions iteratively. ❷ Harnessing-level recursion uses the resulting task-level explorations to update a continual improvement harness. Instead of inheriting the previous execution harness, this improver selectively retains reusable components and lessons about when and why they worked, guiding future proposals and composition.

We evaluate Harness2 on WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench, and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (Team et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Harvey AI, 2026) across four executor–harness configurations. One contrastive step improves performance on all three benchmarks in every configuration, with gains of up to 11.511.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.54.5 points on JobBench, and 11.811.8 percentage points in LAB Partial pass rate. Parallel recursion adds up to 3.93.9 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.24.2 on JobBench, and 6.76.7 percentage points on LAB Partial (Figure 1); the budget study shows gains from both parallel and sequential recursion. Importantly, task-level exploration also benefits subsequent harnessing. Libraries accumulated with a larger recursion budget support stronger subsequent harness edits even without additional probing, and a library transferred from JobBench improves performance on WorkBuddy-Bench (Figure 7). Our contributions are threefold:

  • ①

    Recursive agent harnessing: Harness2 refines the current execution harness and learns from the refinement process to guide future harnessing.

  • ②

    Task-level recursion without ground-truth feedback: We introduce a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step that supports both parallel and sequential recursion.

  • ③

    Experimental results: We demonstrate consistent gains across three benchmarks and four executor–harness configurations, including settings where the same model serves as both executor and editor.

2 Harness2

We first define recursive agent harnessing and its open-world setting (§2.1). We then present task-level recursion for refining the execution harness (§2.2), followed by harnessing-level recursion for updating the improvement harness across tasks (§2.3).

2.2 Task-Level Recursion

Task-level recursion aims to improve the execution harness for the current task. The challenge in our open-world setting is to guide revisions without ground-truth feedback. We therefore introduce a contrastive improvement step that proposes changes, executes them, and examines their behavioral consequences. Building on this step, parallel and sequential recursion use the generated harnesses and execution evidence for further refinement.

2.2.1 A Contrastive Improvement Step

A contrastive step consists of Propose, Probe, and Compose. Let e=(τ,y)e=(\tau,y) denote an execution record, with trajectory τ\tau and deliverable yy. The step applies an improvement operation Φ\Phi to the current execution harness ℋ\mathcal{H} and the available task-local execution and improvement history ℰ\mathcal{E}:

(ℋ′,e′,ξ)=Φ⁡(qt,ℋ,ℰ,ℛt).(\mathcal{H}^{\prime},e^{\prime},\xi)=\Phi(q_{t},\mathcal{H},\mathcal{E};\mathcal{R}_{t}). (1)

It returns a successor harness ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}, its execution record e′e^{\prime}, and a step record ξ\xi containing the reference executions, candidate harnesses and probes, composition decisions, and successor execution. The model and environment are omitted because they stay unchanged; the improvement harness ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} also remains fixed throughout the task.

Propose. The pipeline first obtains a reference execution e0∼𝒜⁡(qt,ℳ,ℋ)e^{0}\sim\mathcal{A}(q_{t};\mathcal{M},\mathcal{H}). Here ∼\sim denotes sampling an execution from the agent. The reference reveals how the harness behaves, not whether its deliverable is correct. Conditioned on the task, current harness, reference, earlier history, and library in ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}, the pipeline proposes two candidates. The invariant candidate targets agentic deficiencies that may recur across domains, such as planning, tool use, context management, or delegation. The domain-specific candidate targets the knowledge, procedures, and constraints of the current domain or environment. Each candidate is an executable harness obtained by editing the current harness’s component files. Proposals may reuse or adapt existing harness components from the library, but task-specific facts must be checked against the current task’s evidence.

Probe. Each candidate harness is executed on the same task under matched model and environment configurations. Comparing its trajectory and deliverable with those of the reference execution yields a behavioral contrast, providing evidence of whether the edits mitigate the targeted deficiency, leave the relevant behavior unchanged, or introduce regressions. These contrasts inform subsequent composition rather than verify task correctness, as execution stochasticity and shared model biases limit the reliability of the evidence.

Compose. The pipeline reads the reference, candidate harnesses, their diffs against the current harness, and all available task-local execution evidence to form the successor ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}. Composition is selective: it may merge supported changes, revise conflicting edits, adopt one candidate, or preserve the current harness. Each decision is tied to a concrete observation rather than a presumed score gain. The composed harness is then executed to produce e′e^{\prime}, and the decisions and their evidence are recorded in ξ\xi. The step therefore returns an executed successor together with the evidence and decisions behind its refinement.

2.2.2 Parallel and Sequential Recursion

Building on the contrastive improvement step, we introduce two forms of task-level recursion (Figure 4): parallel recursion composes refinements from multiple candidate harnesses and their executions, while sequential recursion carries the refined harness and execution evidence into subsequent steps. A positive integer kk controls the exploration budget: kk candidates per scope and kk compositions in parallel, or kk chained steps in sequence. The improvement harness ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} remains fixed throughout.

Parallel Recursion. Parallel recursion follows the aggregation principle of RSA (Venkatraman et al., 2025), but operates on executable harnesses and their behavioral consequences rather than reasoning outputs. The pipeline collects kk reference executions of the current harness ℋ\mathcal{H}, then independently proposes and probes kk invariant and kk domain-specific candidates. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} denote the reference executions and 𝒫\mathcal{P} the pool of candidate harnesses paired with their execution records. Each of kk independent composition sessions receives the full pool:

ℋj′=Composej(qt,ℋ,ℬ,𝒫;ℛt),j=1,…,k.\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{j}=\textsc{Compose}_{j}(q_{t},\mathcal{H},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{P};\mathcal{R}_{t}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,k. (2)

Each session selectively combines or revises supported edits to produce a successor ℋj′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{j}, which is then executed. The recursive update thus uses generated harnesses and execution evidence for further refinement, not merely output ranking. Our implementation performs one population update; kk controls its width rather than its depth.

Sequential Recursion. Sequential recursion applies iterative self-refinement (Madaan et al., 2023) to the execution harness. Starting from ℋ(0)=ℋ0\mathcal{H}^{(0)}=\mathcal{H}_{0}, it chains kk contrastive steps, each conditioned on the preceding harness and accumulated execution history ℰ(r−1)\mathcal{E}^{(r-1)}:

(ℋ(r),e(r),ξ(r))=Φ(qt,ℋ(r−1),ℰ(r−1);ℛt),r=1,…,k.(\mathcal{H}^{(r)},e^{(r)},\xi^{(r)})=\Phi(q_{t},\mathcal{H}^{(r-1)},\mathcal{E}^{(r-1)};\mathcal{R}_{t}),\qquad r=1,\ldots,k. (3)

Here, Φ\Phi is the contrastive step defined in Equation 1, returning the refined harness, its execution record e(r)e^{(r)}, and the step record ξ(r)\xi^{(r)}. The initial history contains kk base executions and is extended after each step with ξ(r)\xi^{(r)}. Later steps can therefore retain, revise, or correct earlier changes using both current and previous evidence.

Final Selection. For k>1k>1, an agentic selector compares anonymized deliverables against the task request and source materials. It returns an existing output without access to its originating harness or synthesizing new content. The corresponding harness is denoted ℋt⋆\mathcal{H}_{t}^{\star}, where the star indicates adoption rather than verified optimality. Selection adds no harness revision. At k=1k=1, both forms reduce to the basic contrastive step and bypass selection. Appendix H provides the stage prompts.

4 Analysis

We analyze Harness2 along six lines: the effect of task-level recursion under increasing budget; the compute–performance trade-off; an ablation of the library, the scoped candidates, and composition; library generalization without execution, across benchmarks, and across tasks; the same model as improver and executor; and a case study. Additional analyses are presented in Appendix E.

Effect of Task-Level Recursion. Figure 5 compares parallel and sequential recursion on WB-code and WB-office. Both improve monotonically as kk increases from 11 to 55.

Parallel recursion rises from 76.576.5 to 80.880.8 on Code and from 79.579.5 to 83.483.4 on Office. In contrast, ReasoningBank and Harness Scaling show smaller or inconsistent gains as kk increases. Harness Scaling regresses from k=2k{=}2 to 33 on both domains, while ReasoningBank fluctuates. Notably, both recursive forms of Harness2 at k=2k{=}2 outperform every plotted baseline at k=5k{=}5 on both domains. Parallel recursion finishes above sequential recursion at k=5k{=}5, although sequential recursion is higher on Code at k=2k{=}2. Increasing test-time exploration alone therefore does not ensure better performance; recursive harness refinement produces more consistent gains in these settings. Parallel proposal and composition sessions can run concurrently; realized latency also depends on available concurrency and rollout duration.

Compute–Performance Trade-off. Figure 6 compares performance and total compute on JobBench and WorkBuddy-Bench, counting all tokens spent before the final deliverable is submitted. Both evaluated Harness2 configurations lie on the empirical Pareto frontier. With Gemini 3.5 Flash under OpenCode, increasing kk from 11 to 55 raises gains over the base from 4.54.5 to 7.57.5 points on JobBench and from 5.15.1 to 8.48.4 on WorkBuddy-Bench. ReasoningBank and Harness Scaling yield smaller gains, while Meta-Harness uses more compute than Harness2 at k=5k{=}5 for lower performance. This comparison includes both execution and improvement costs.

Ablation Study. We ablate three components of Harness2: (i) the harness improvement library of §2.3, (ii) the scoped editor roles, and (iii) composition. Experiments are conducted on WorkBuddy-Bench, averaged over its three domains, and on JobBench, with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the executor under the OpenCode harness at k=1k{=}1, so that each component is isolated from the test-time budget of §2.2.2.

w/o library improves each task as before but neither reads from nor writes to the improvement library, so no task benefits from what earlier ones tried. w/o scoping replaces the invariant and domain editors with two generic ones, so the same number of candidates is drafted from the same evidence and probed under the same budget, but neither reads the trajectory at a stated scope. w/o composition probes both candidates and then skips composition, returning whichever the evidence favours, so the two proposals remain alternatives rather than parts. Table 3 shows that removing the library lowers WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench scores by 3.13.1 and 1.81.8 points, respectively; removing scoping costs 2.92.9 and 3.73.7, and removing composition costs 1.61.6 and 1.91.9. All three components contribute to performance. Appendix E.1 further evaluates removing prompt-related components, skills, and scripts from the improved harness.

Analysis of Harnessing-Level Recursion. We investigate whether updating a continual improvement harness enhances subsequent refinement and how this benefit scales with task-level exploration. Figure 7 (left) shows that directly refining the base execution harness without access to reference executions, candidate probes, or the improvement library degrades performance on Code and Web. Specifically, Code scores drop from 73.473.4 to 63.263.2 and Web scores fall from 69.969.9 to 65.065.0. An improvement library accumulated at k=1k{=}1 restores base performance.

With k=5k{=}5, the library instead supports gains of 0.90.9, 4.44.4, and 5.15.1 points on Code, Web, and Office. Greater task-level exploration thus benefits subsequent harnessing without further probing. A JobBench-derived library also improves one-step refinement on WorkBuddy-Bench by 0.60.6, 0.50.5, and 2.92.9 points, respectively (Figure 7, right). Excluding each task’s own library entry yields gains of 1.91.9 points on WorkBuddy-Bench and 1.71.7 on JobBench (Figure 11). This retrospective test uses later-task experience to evaluate cross-task reuse, not online adaptation. Appendix E analyzes component reuse.

Same Model as Executor and Editor. To test whether gains require a stronger editor, we use the same model for both roles with OpenCode at k=2k{=}2 (Figure 8). All five models, from GLM-5 to Claude Opus 5, improve on every benchmark. Opus 5 gains 3.33.3, 5.55.5, and 3.03.0 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench, and LAB; GLM-5 gains 13.713.7 points on LAB. These results demonstrate that harness refinement need not rely on a stronger editor. Appendix E.3 evaluates transfer to other executor models.

Case Study. Figure 9 presents a JobBench task evaluated using Gemini 3.5 Flash and OpenCode (additional examples across all benchmarks and domains are available in Appendix E.7). The baseline run scored 43.143.1. Its trajectory revealed procedural failures rather than knowledge gaps: data was never reconciled across source files, and outputs were never reopened for verification after being written. To resolve this, two targeted interventions were applied. First, the invariant intervention acts as a process-level guardrail, forcing the model to inventory all inputs, trace figures to their exact sources, and use a verification script to reopen and check produced files. Second, the domain intervention introduces a specialized skill providing reconciliation mechanics for schedule, venue, labor, and budget files, alongside tool guidance for handling specific number formats. When evaluated against the reference, the Composer retained all four edits introduced by the two interventions. The optimized re-run successfully cross-referenced the figures and restored the memo’s missing sections, raising the score to 77.877.8.

Appendix B Benchmarks

WorkBuddy-Bench (Team et al., 2026) contains three domains as separate datasets: Code (8080 tasks over five role categories: developer, algorithms, product, operations, and QA), Web (7070 tasks over seven categories such as page interaction, data visualization, and document conversion), and Office (5050 tasks over data-file operations, document operations, and workspace automation). Each dataset is split in half by category, and we report on the test halves (40/35/2540/35/25 tasks). Tasks run in the benchmark’s containers; the executor’s harness is mounted into the container and every rollout is a fresh container. Grading is the benchmark’s composite verifier: deterministic checks (hidden tests, file and structure checks) combined with LLM and VLM judge items, with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the judge model where one is needed; the score of a task is the fraction of its checks that pass. The verifier never exposes its expected values to any model in our pipeline.

JobBench (Li et al., 2026) contains 6565 professional tasks, each with input documents and a set of requested deliverables, grouped into seven occupational domains. We use a frozen 31/3431/34 split and report on the 3434 test tasks. Deliverables are judged against a weighted rubric by Claude Opus 4.8; the task score is the total weighted score over the maximum score, which is the benchmark’s own metric. The rubric is never shown to the executor, the editor, or the selector.

LAB (Harvey AI, 2026) is Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark: 1,2511{,}251 legal tasks across 2424 practice areas and four work types (analyse, draft, review, research), each scored by an LLM judge against per-task criteria, with no executable check. We follow the split of the harness-optimization study (Niklaus, 2026), which applied Meta-Harness to LAB and froze two disjoint sets: a 100100-task held-out test set, stratified by practice area and forced to cover all four work types and the full range of context sizes (including one matter above a million tokens), and a 2424-task dev set with one task per practice area for fast iteration. Every LAB number in this paper is on the 100100 test tasks, which each method processes as one stream; the 2424 dev tasks are used only by Meta-Harness as its search set. Tasks are judged by Claude Sonnet 4.6, and we report the per-criterion pass rate (Partial).

The train halves of WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench are used by Meta-Harness alone, as its offline setting. Harness2 and the other baselines never use them: they process the test tasks as a stream, starting from an empty library or memory. Each reported score is the mean over three independent streams, and #Steps is the number of model turns in the executor’s session.

Appendix H Prompts

⬇
(*@\textit{Opening line:}@*)
You are composing checkpoint (*@$t$ of $k$@*) in a sequential adaptation loop.
(*@\textit{Evidence paragraph:}@*)
The rollouts under the unmodified harness (the shared evidence, which does not change between rounds), this round’s INV and DOM candidates with their rollouts, and every earlier round’s candidates, checkpoints and trajectories. The previous checkpoint’s own rollout is this round’s on-policy evidence: it shows what the harness you are editing actually does.
(*@\textit{Composition options:}@*)
Compose checkpoint (*@$t$@*), which the next round will build on.
All of these are valid:
- MERGE across rounds – including a candidate REJECTED earlier, if a later rollout now argues for it.
- REPRODUCE an earlier checkpoint verbatim, if that state was simply the best one and later rounds drifted away from it.
- ADOPT this round’s best candidate.
(*@\textit{In place of the parallel-aggregator note and the process slot:}@*)
Here ‘KEEP_BASE‘ means keep the CURRENT checkpoint in ‘context/harness/‘ unchanged; it does not restore the original harness. In ‘<notes>‘, identify which rounds’ edits survive and which were dropped or restored.
